newsitem.title: USA: Students, office workers, moms leading women online.
newsitem.headline: Students, office workers, moms leading women online.

text.p: Trend setters are easy to spot. They're the people who dine at restaurants before they're chic, know all the up and coming bands, and wear styles a season ahead of the crowd.
Computer trend setters are easy to spot, too. They were the first on their block to bring home a PC, first to plug a modem into it, and first to use the Internet.

Some "techie" trend setters are women, and this summer Forrester Research interviewed 100 of them to draw a bead on how women will be using the Internet and online services this year and through the turn of the century.
The research outfit in Cambridge, Mass., predicts that more than 18 million women in the United States will be "wired" by the year 2000.

Forrester used interviews of so-called "early adapters," plus previous statistical analysis and additional research from Internet service providers and content developers to identify trends and help companies predict what Internet products and services might be popular because of them.
According to Forrester analyst Kate Delhagen, women's online use is being spearheaded by three groups:
-- College students, who are more likely than ever to bring a modem-equipped computer with them to campus and use the Internet for classes and communication;
-- Working women employed by companies building corporate intranets, internal computer networks based on Internet protocols;
-- Stay-at-home moms who've stopped watching "Oprah" during the kids' nap time to log on and chat with friends, balance their checkbook or read an electronic newspaper.

These women are most likely to use their Internet accounts or America Online subscriptions to send e-mail, track the news, browse the Web, chat and take classes. Their biggest obstacles to getting online are lack of time, equipment and money, according to Forrester.

As the Internet moves from being a "Gen-X" hangout to a mass medium, major consumer marketers are beginning to set up shop. Delhagen predicts a continued increase in the number of companies setting up Web sites targeting women.

Some of those companies include publishers Conde Nast, whose Epicurious (http://travel.epicurious.com/) travel site offers a travel-planning concierge and destination database, and Hearst, whose HomeArts (http://homearts.com/) site includes a searchable database of 2,000 recipes.
Another is Clinique, which has launched a Web site (http://www.clinique.com/) and will offer Internet tutorials and give away software at its department store cosmetics counters.

But not all women want to go online to find out about cooking or skin care. Forty-four percent of the "early adapters" Forrester surveyed said there was no difference between what men and women do online.

Some of the most popular sites among female Internet trend setters aren't targeted to women. Instead, they provide information or services in a gender-neutral setting that make women feel comfortable, Delhagen said.

Among these services are Match.com (http://www.match.com), an online dating service, and Auto-By-Tel (http://www.autobytel.com/), which matches prospective car buyers with price-conscious dealers in their area.

"Buying a car is a great example of a situation where a woman may not feel comfortable," Delhagen said. "Auto-By-Tel neutralises the process. It's a use of the medium that you can't do anywhere else."
Web sites that help people find jobs or take classes create the same type of safe zones, and should also attract a large female audience, Delhagen said.

Other gender-neutral Web sites that Forrester identified as benefiting women include electronic communities SeniorNet (http://www.seniornet.org/), which targets older adults, and Tripod (http://www.tripod.com/), set up to help twentysomethings deal with jobs, roommates, relationships and other early-adult issues.
Delhagen also has high hopes for WOW Factor (http://www.wowfactor.com/), a launch pad that's set to debut shortly to help female small-business owners get onto the Internet.
"They recognise small-business owners don't know where to start" on the Web, Delhagen said. "That's not unique to women, but they've decided to outreach to that group."

Although pollsters such as Nielsen and FIND have done a good job tracking how many people use the Internet, less has been done until now to track what people, female and male, do once they're logged on, Delhagen said.

"There's a lack of knowledge," she said. "This whole market has exploded. There's a lot of money at stake from all kinds of companies and industries. People's careers hinge on whether this takes off."
Speaking of careers, the Internet is also providing fantastic job opportunities for women, comparable with the early days of the cable television industry, Delhagen said.
"A lot of traditional industries are losing their best, most seasoned talent to this new world. We seem some big career shifts happening," she said.
(Michelle V. Rafter writes about cyberspace and technology from Los Angeles. Reach her at mvrafter@deltanet.com. Opinions expressed in this column are her own.)
